To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
increased intracellular calcium concentration and activation of protein kinase do not affect the Na+ and water permeabilities of the rat cortical collecting tubule.
elevation of [Ca2+]I and activation of PKC do not affect Na+ and water reabsorption in the rat CCD.

(1) AVP increases Na+ and water permeability in the rat CCD; (2) the increase in Na+ permeability is due to an increase in the number of Na+ channels; and (3) the increase in water permeability is due, in part, to an increase in aquaporin-2 water channels.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms that regulate sodium and water transport across epithelia.
the role of calcium and protein kinase C in the regulation of sodium and water transport in renal epithelia.
the regulation of sodium and water transport by the cortical collecting duct (CD).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Ca(2+)-dependent PKC activation does not affect Na(+) and water transport in CCD, and that Ca(2+) itself may not have a role in the regulation of these processes in this nephron segment.
Ca2+ does not appear to be involved with the regulation of water transport across the CCD.
Ca2+ and protein kinase C (both increased) do not inhibit NaCl and water transport in CCD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Ca2+ and protein kinase C (Ca2+/PKC) are not important in the regulation of Na+ and water absorption in the CCD.
Ca(2+) and PKC are not required for the regulation of Na(+) and water transport in CCD.
the Ca2+ signal transduction pathway is not involved in the regulation of Na+ and water reabsorption in the rat CCD.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ca2+ and protein kinase C (which are activated by vasopressin) do not inhibit Na transport in the CCD, which may explain the sustained increase in Na transport that we observe with vasopressin.
the effects of AVP on Na+ transport in the rat CCD do not appear to be mediated by PKC activation or increased [Ca2+].
we have demonstrated that the effects of AVP are not mediated through PKC or Ca2+ signaling.
